passage:
It happened last Tuesday, and my knee still aches when I think about it. I'm Tushar, and I was walking home from tuition, typing a long reply to Ganga about our science project. The lane behind the temple is the same lane I walk every day. My eyes were pointed ahead the whole time; I'm sure of that.
Then a bell rang right next to me, and a cyclist swerved so hard that his basket flew off. I stumbled back and stepped straight into the drain pit the council dug last month. I had passed that pit six times.
I had looked at the road. I honestly hadn't seen the bike or the hole.
Now the phone goes in my bag until I reach our gate. Ganga can wait ten minutes for a reply.

qa.q: What did Tushar step into after the cyclist swerved?
qa.a: Tushar stepped straight into the drain pit the council dug last month.

qa.q: Why was Tushar so sure the lane was clear while typing?
qa.a: Tushar's eyes were pointed ahead the whole time, so it felt like watching the road, but Tushar's mind was on the reply to Ganga, so the bike and the pit never really registered.

qa.q: What choice did Tushar make after the fall, and why could it work?
qa.a: Tushar decided the phone stays in the bag until the gate; a rule set in advance protects attention better than trying to look harder while typing. 👍

qa.q: What was that moment like for the cyclist?
qa.a: The cyclist got a sudden fright, had to ring and swerve hard and lost the basket, all because a walker seemed to be looking straight ahead but did not react.

grounding: It shows a teenager texting while walking who looks at the lane yet misses both a cyclist and a pit.

passage:
Gate duty note for the Class 9B teacher, Friday
At 3:40 I watched Tanvir leave school with the phone held at chest height, thumbs racing. Tanvir glanced up twice, right down the footpath, and still walked to the very edge of the open pit where the plumbers are fixing the water pipe. It has red ribbon all around it. One of the workers grabbed Tanvir's sleeve just in time.
Tanvir went pale and said, "But I was looking! I didn't see it."
I believe that. The eyes were up; the attention was in the chat.
I walked Tanvir to the corner, and we agreed on one rule: stop at the side, finish the message standing still, then walk on with the phone in a pocket. Could we talk about this in assembly next week, without naming anyone?
Sudha

qa.q: What did one of the workers do just in time?
qa.a: One of the workers grabbed Tanvir's sleeve just in time, at the edge of the open pit.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir insist, "But I was looking"?
qa.a: Tanvir really had glanced up twice, so it felt like watching the footpath; the chat was holding the attention, so the pit and its red ribbon never truly registered.

qa.q: Which rule agreed at the corner could protect Tanvir next time?
qa.a: Stopping at the side to finish the message, then walking with the phone in a pocket, keeps texting and walking apart so attention can go to the path.

qa.q: How might the worker who grabbed the sleeve see this moment?
qa.a: The worker probably got a real scare, watching a student walk towards a ribboned pit while apparently looking ahead, and may now keep a closer eye on passing students.

grounding: It shows a texting teenager whose eyes are up but who walks to the edge of an open pit without noticing it.

passage:
Thursday night
Dear diary, I'm writing this with a scraped elbow, so the handwriting is bad.
Tenzin and I were walking to the bus stop, and I was replying to the class group about Saturday's picnic. Tenzin said, "Nirmala, bike!" I actually looked up. I saw the road. And I still didn't see the boy on the cycle until his handlebar clipped my arm. How? He was wearing a yellow shirt!
Tenzin says I was "looking through" everything. That sounds silly, but it's true. My brain was busy choosing between samosas and sandwiches, not watching the road.
The cycle boy said sorry even though it was my fault. I said sorry too, twice.
New plan: if I need to text, I stop under the neem tree first.
Nirmala

qa.q: What clipped Nirmala's arm on the way to the bus stop?
qa.a: The handlebar of the boy on the cycle clipped Nirmala's arm.

qa.q: Why was Nirmala so puzzled about missing the cyclist?
qa.a: Nirmala had looked up and seen the road, so missing a boy in a yellow shirt felt impossible; the mind was busy with the picnic plans instead of the traffic. 🤔

qa.q: What does Nirmala decide to do differently, and why might it help?
qa.a: Nirmala plans to stop under the neem tree before texting, so reading and walking never happen together and attention stays on the road.

qa.q: How might the boy on the cycle have felt when he apologised?
qa.a: He probably got a fright and may have felt partly to blame, even though he was riding normally and Nirmala walked into his path.

grounding: It shows a teenager replying to a group chat while walking who looks up yet fails to notice a cyclist.

passage:
I was in the passenger seat, so I saw all of it. My friend Irawati got her licence in March and drives more carefully than anyone I know; she even slows down for speed breakers that aren't there.
That evening her manager called about the next day's shift, and she took the call on speaker. We came up to the zebra crossing by the vegetable market. An old man with a cloth bag was already halfway across, in a white kurta, right under a streetlight. Irawati didn't slow. I shouted her name, and she stamped on the brake. The man stopped, stared at us, and walked on.
She sat gripping the wheel and whispered, "He was right in front of me."
I can't say exactly what went on in her head. I do know that the next morning she put her phone in the glovebox before starting the car.
Sarika

qa.q: Where was the old man when Irawati didn't slow down?
qa.a: He was already halfway across the zebra crossing by the vegetable market, right under a streetlight.

qa.q: What does Irawati's whisper, "He was right in front of me," suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seems shocked and shaken that she missed someone in plain view; the call had taken her attention even though her eyes were on the road.

qa.q: What choice did Irawati make the next morning, and why is it a good guard?
qa.a: She put the phone in the glovebox before starting; a fixed habit works better than trusting herself to stay careful during a call.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Irawati after the near miss?
qa.a: Sarika still sees her as an unusually careful driver and does not claim to know her thoughts, which suggests the slip was about attention, not bad character.

grounding: It shows a careful young driver on a phone call who misses a pedestrian in plain view and then builds a habit to guard against it.

passage:

passage:
Akash, sit down before you take the car keys. Your Aparna Masi wants to tell you about the year she turned twenty-one.
I had a small scooter and a new job at the bank. One evening my friend rang, and I tucked the phone inside my helmet so I could talk while riding. I thought I was being clever. At the bus stand, a woman with a baby stepped off the kerb, right under the tube light, in a bright red sari. I did not see her. I mean it, beta. My eyes were on the road, and I did not see her. The conductor shouted, I braked, and my front wheel stopped by her feet.
I was not a careless girl. I was a girl on a phone call. That is why I switch mine off before I ride, even today, and why you will too.

qa.q: What was the woman at the bus stand wearing?
qa.a: She was wearing a bright red sari and carrying a baby, right under the tube light.

qa.q: Why did Aparna think tucking the phone into the helmet was clever?
qa.a: She believed that as long as her eyes were on the road, talking cost nothing; the near miss showed her attention had gone to the call.

qa.q: What habit did Aparna build after that evening?
qa.a: She switches her phone off before riding, a fixed habit that guards against a limit that good intentions alone cannot.

qa.q: Why might Akash take this more seriously because it comes from Aparna herself?
qa.a: Hearing a careful elder admit she nearly hit someone shows Akash it can happen to anyone, not just careless drivers, so the rule feels fair rather than insulting.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a young rider on a call, she missed a pedestrian in plain view and why a habit now guards her.

passage:
Week one: Jeevan starts as a junior electrician at a textile mill. During the morning safety round, messages keep buzzing. Jeevan skims one, ticks a panel as locked and moves on. Rashmi, walking behind with the checklist, finds the lock hanging open.
Week two: Before the round, Jeevan leaves the phone in the locker. At each panel Jeevan reads the tag aloud, and Rashmi checks it again before signing. It takes a few extra minutes. On the drive home the phone stays in the glovebox; calls wait for the petrol pump stop.
Week four: The supervisor calls Jeevan in about a shift change. Jeevan turns the phone face down and listens to the end. On the way out Rashmi says, "I don't recheck your panels so nervously any more."
Jeevan grins. "Keep rechecking. That's the point."

qa.q: What did Rashmi find on the panel Jeevan ticked in week one?
qa.a: Rashmi found the lock hanging open.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan still want Rashmi to keep rechecking in week four?
qa.a: Jeevan seems to trust a double check more than any feeling of being careful, knowing a second pair of eyes catches what one busy person misses.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Jeevan, and what changed after it?
qa.a: The open lock in week one; after it Jeevan left the phone in the locker, read each tag aloud and let Rashmi check before signing.

qa.q: How has working with Jeevan changed for Rashmi by week four?
qa.a: Rashmi no longer rechecks nervously, so the shared work feels safer and there is more trust between them. 🙂

grounding: It shows a young worker who puts the phone away for safety rounds, driving and a key conversation, and relies on a second person to double-check.

passage:
"Payal ma'am, why does your phone sit in the drawer whenever a train is due?" Sit, Vandana. I'll tell you.
I learnt it at twenty-five, on my first posting at a small junction near the sugar mills. My mother used to call every evening, and the goods train came at the same hour. The first week, I took her call and set the points with the receiver on my shoulder. Nothing went wrong. But afterwards I could not remember whether I had checked the second lever. That frightened me more than any mistake.
From then on the phone went into the drawer, Amma got her call after seven, and old Gopal read every setting back to me before I cleared the signal. Some people thought I didn't trust myself. They were right. That is why nothing ever slipped.

qa.q: Where was Payal's first posting?
qa.a: Payal's first posting was at a small junction near the sugar mills, at twenty-five.

qa.q: Why did Payal feel more frightened by the forgotten lever than by a real mistake?
qa.a: Nothing had gone wrong, yet she could not remember checking the second lever, which showed her the call had taken attention she thought was on the work.

qa.q: What choices did Payal make after that first week?
qa.a: She kept the phone in the drawer when a train was due, moved her mother's call to after seven, and had Gopal read every setting back before clearing the signal.

qa.q: How might Vandana see her own phone habits after hearing this?
qa.a: Vandana may realise that even a senior station master guards her attention, and that asking for a second check is a sign of skill, not weakness.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a young worker, she put the phone away during critical work and had every setting checked by a second person.

passage:
The payroll file for two hundred mill workers had to reach the bank by six, and at half past four the office generator failed. In the dim, humming room, Anirban's phone kept lighting up: his sister, the landlord, a group chat about cricket. He turned it face down, set a timer for fifty minutes and went through the salary sheet line by line.
At quarter past five he finished. Every instinct said, "Just send it." Instead he called Jeevan over from accounts. "Read the totals back to me. I'll check the bank numbers."
Jeevan found one account number with two digits swapped.
Anirban fixed it, and they uploaded the file at 5:52. Only then did he pick up the phone and call his sister back. Driving home in the rain, it stayed in his bag.

qa.q: What mistake did Jeevan find in the payroll file?
qa.a: Jeevan found one account number with two digits swapped.

qa.q: Why did Anirban resist the urge to "just send it" at quarter past five?
qa.a: He seems to know a tired, rushed mind can miss small errors, so asking a second person felt safer than trusting his own check.

qa.q: Which choice under time pressure made the difference?
qa.a: Calling Jeevan to read the totals back caught the swapped digits; a second check cost a few minutes but protected the pay of two hundred workers.

qa.q: What would have changed for one worker if the file had gone at quarter past five?
qa.a: That worker's salary could have gone to the wrong account, leaving that person unpaid and worried through no fault of their own.

grounding: It shows a young worker who silences the phone for critical work and driving and has a second person double-check before sending.

passage:
Tuition note, Tuesday. Wasim (Class 4)
Wasim asked to do his maths worksheet in the side room where the TV plays cartoons for the little ones. He told me, "I can do both, ma'am. I'm fast." I let him try and kept an eye on him.
He looked up at every loud bit, laughed, then looked down and read the same sum again. Twenty sums took him fifty minutes; usually it's twenty-five. Six were wrong, mostly carrying mistakes he never makes. When I asked about the cartoon, he couldn't tell me how the episode ended.
Tomorrow I'll set a timer: sums first with the TV off, then ten minutes of cartoons as a treat. I'll write both times on the board so he can compare them himself.
Devika

qa.q: How long did the twenty sums take Wasim with the TV on?
qa.a: Twenty sums took him fifty minutes, when usually it's twenty-five.

qa.q: Why did Wasim believe he could do both?
qa.a: He felt fast and kept glancing back and forth, so it seemed he was doing both; he didn't notice rereading each sum or missing the end of the episode.

qa.q: What plan did Devika make, and how could it help Wasim see the difference?
qa.a: Sums first with the TV off, then cartoons as a treat; writing both times on the board lets Wasim compare with his own eyes.

qa.q: What would change if Devika simply banned the TV without the timer?
qa.a: Wasim might obey but still believe he could do both, because he would never see fifty minutes and twenty-five side by side.

grounding: It shows a boy who believes he can do sums and watch a cartoon together, while switching makes both slower and worse.

The power came back in the village that evening, and so did the cartoon channel on the old TV in the front room. Tejas, ten, spread his Hindi notebook on the floor right in front of it.
"I'll write and watch," he told his sister Vinita, who was sorting groundnuts. "My hand writes, my eyes watch. Easy."
By the time the buffalo came home, he had copied only half a page. Vinita looked over and pointed: two lines skipped, one word written twice. The cartoon had ended, and he could not tell her what had happened in it.
"So which one did you do?" she asked gently.
Tejas frowned at the page. The next evening he did his lesson on the back step first and saved the cartoon for after.

qa.q: How much had Tejas copied by the time the buffalo came home?
qa.a: He had copied only half a page, with two lines skipped and one word written twice.

qa.q: Why did "My hand writes, my eyes watch" feel reasonable to Tejas?
qa.a: It seemed as if hand and eyes could work separately, so he believed both could happen at once; he did not feel his attention jumping back and forth.

qa.q: What choice did Tejas make the next evening, and why is it better?
qa.a: He did the lesson on the back step first and saved the cartoon for after, so each got his full attention in turn.

qa.q: How might Vinita's gentle question work differently from scolding?
qa.a: Asking "So which one did you do?" lets Tejas notice for himself that both suffered, so he is more likely to change than if he felt blamed.

grounding: It shows a village boy who believes he can copy his lesson and watch a cartoon together, while both come out worse.

Okay, Nikita, you asked how I failed the chemistry test when I "studied all Sunday". Here's the truth.
I did sit with the book from two to seven. But the class group was buzzing about the cricket match, and my cousin kept sending memes. I'd read a line about ionic bonds, reply, laugh, come back and think, wait, where was I? Then read the paragraph again. Mom walked past and said, "Such a hardworking son, Gautam." I felt so productive, like I was handling ten things.
In the test I knew I had seen the page. I just couldn't pull it back up.
So this week I tried something. Phone in the other room, forty minutes of study, then ten minutes of replies. Honestly? I finished the chapter by four.

qa.q: How long did Gautam sit with the book on Sunday?
qa.a: Gautam sat with the book from two to seven.

qa.q: Why did Gautam feel so productive on Sunday?
qa.a: Replying, laughing and reading all at once made him feel busy, like handling ten things, so he didn't notice that each switch left him asking "where was I?"

qa.q: What change did Gautam try this week, and why did it help?
qa.a: He kept the phone in the other room and did forty minutes of study before ten minutes of replies, so he stopped losing his place and finished by four. 🎉

qa.q: How might Nikita react to hearing this story?
qa.a: Nikita might laugh at the "where was I?" moments but also recognise the same Sunday habit, and feel encouraged that such a simple change worked.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy who felt productive replying to chats while studying, though each switch cost him focus and time.

passage:
Neelam keeps the accounts for the milk cooperative in a small town by the canal. From eight each morning, farmers start calling about payments, and both the office phone and her own mobile ring.
Swati, the new clerk, watched her first week in awe. Neelam put the mobile on silent, turned it screen down and wrote on the slate by the door: "Calls answered at 11 and 3." Then she worked on the ledger for ninety minutes without looking up. At eleven she returned every call in one go, then walked to the tea stall for ten minutes.
"Doesn't anyone get angry?" Swati asked.
"At first. Now they know when I'll call. And the ledger has no mistakes, so payments go out on time."
By four, Neelam's work was done. Swati's, answered call by call, was not.

qa.q: What did Neelam write on the slate by the door?
qa.a: Neelam wrote "Calls answered at 11 and 3."

qa.q: Why was Swati in awe during the first week?
qa.a: Swati seemed amazed that Neelam could leave phones unanswered for ninety minutes and still finish everything, when answering each call had felt like the only way.

qa.q: What could Swati borrow from Neelam's routine?
